records.title: Amide proton transfer of carnosine in aqueous solution studied in vitro by WEX and CEST experiments.
records.quote: We show that the metabolite carnosine creates a CEST effect and we study the properties of the exchange of the amide proton (-NH) of the carnosine peptide bond (NHCPB) in model solutions for a pH range from 6 to 8.3 and a temperature range from T = 5 °C to 43 °C by means of CEST and water exchange spectroscopy (WEX) experiments on a 3 T whole-body MR tomograph. The dependence of the NHCPB chemical exchange rate k(sw) on pH and temperature T was determined using WEX. For physiological conditions (T = 37 °C, pH = 7.10) we obtained k(sw) = (47.07 ± 7.90)/s.

records.notes: Rate is for creatine, not PCr, but included because PCr is co-mapped and the abstract gives PCrCEST-specific B1 optimum. Peak offsets not stated in abstract.

records.title: The exchange rate of creatine CEST in mouse brain.
records.quote: The CrCEST exchange rate was found to be around 240-480 s-1 in the mouse brain, which is significantly lower than that in solutions (∼1000 s-1 ).
records.metabolite_or_pool: Creatine guanidinium (CrCEST) — comparator for PCr (GUANIDINIUM group, cross-listed)

records.title: Amplified detection of phosphocreatine and creatine after supplementation using CEST MRI at high and ultrahigh magnetic fields.
records.quote: We were furthermore interested in determining the limiting conditions for distinguishing between creatine (1.9 ppm) and phosphocreatine (2.6 ppm) signals at ultra-high fields (21 T) and determine their concentrations could be reliably obtained using Bloch equation fits of the experimental CEST spectra.
records.metabolite_or_pool: PHOSPHOCREATINE NH (2.6 ppm) and creatine (1.9 ppm)
records.conditions: hind limb muscle and kidneys in vivo (species not stated in abstract) at 11.7 T and 21.1 T, before/after IV PCr; pH/temperature not stated in abstract
records.notes: Kidney PCr CEST at 2.6 ppm increased up to 4% after administration (exogenous PCr). Exchange rate not stated.

records.title: Creatine and phosphocreatine mapping of mouse skeletal muscle by a polynomial and Lorentzian line-shape fitting CEST method.

records.notes: A separate sentence of the same abstract (not quoted) says the in vivo Lorentzian fits used peaks at 1.95 ppm and 2.5 ppm. Muscle showed no protein guanidinium peak, unlike brain. No exchange rate stated.

records.title: pH Mapping of Skeletal Muscle by Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (CEST) Imaging.
records.quote: The measured CEST signal ratio was between 1.96 ppm and 2.6 ppm in the z-spectrum, and this was associated with pH values based on the ratio between the creatine (Cr) and the phosphocreatine (PCr).
records.metabolite_or_pool: PHOSPHOCREATINE (2.6 ppm) / creatine (1.96 ppm) ratio

records.notes: No exchange rate stated.

records.title: Quantitative assessment of cardiac phosphocreatine metabolism under physiological and pharmacological stress using chemical exchange saturation transfer magnetic resonance imaging.

records.notes: Three-pool Bloch-McConnell fit (water, PCr, MT). Human myocardial [PCr]d 13.2 ± 1.4 mM at rest by CEST vs 12.9 ± 1.4 mM by 31P-MRS. Exchange rate not numerically stated.

records.title: Chemical exchange rotation transfer imaging of phosphocreatine in muscle.
records.quote: In chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) imaging, the signal at 2.6 ppm from the water resonance in muscle has been assigned to phosphocreatine (PCr).

records.notes: CERT metric AREXdouble,cpw at 2.6 ppm; PCr dominates but baseline contributions are 'nontrivial'. No exchange rate stated.

records.title: A rapid method for phosphocreatine-weighted imaging in muscle using double saturation power-chemical exchange saturation transfer.

records.notes: Residual MT and aromatic NOE contamination acknowledged. No exchange rate stated.

records.title: Exchange rates of creatine kinase metabolites: feasibility of imaging creatine by chemical exchange saturation transfer MRI.

records.title: Quantitative chemical exchange saturation transfer MRI of intervertebral disc in a porcine model.
records.quote: In the animal studies, the relationship can be described as ksw  =9.2 × 106 × 10-pH + 196.9, R2  = 0.7883.

records.title: Chemical exchange saturation transfer magnetic resonance imaging of human knee cartilage at 3 T and 7 T.

records.title: Cartilage quality assessment by using glycosaminoglycan chemical exchange saturation transfer and (23)Na MR imaging at 7 T.

records.title: Characterization of viscosupplementation formulations using chemical exchange saturation transfer (ViscoCEST).

records.title: Diamagnetic chemical exchange saturation transfer (diaCEST) affords magnetic resonance imaging of extracellular matrix hydrogel implantation in a rat model of stroke.

records.title: Investigating hydroxyl chemical exchange using a variable saturation power chemical exchange saturation transfer (vCEST) method at 3 T.

records.title: Optimization of 7-T chemical exchange saturation transfer parameters for validation of glycosaminoglycan and amide proton transfer of fibroglandular breast tissue.
records.quote: By using these parameters, reproducible values were obtained for both the amide and hydroxyl protons from CEST MR imaging at 7 T and are feasible in the human breast.

records.notes: Non-cartilage GAG hydroxyl CEST in humans; no rate or offset stated in abstract.

records.title: Transforming thymidine into a magnetic resonance imaging probe for monitoring gene expression.

records.title: Breast cancer redox heterogeneity detectable with chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI.

records.title: Molecular Imaging of Deoxycytidine Kinase Activity Using Deoxycytidine-Enhanced CEST MRI.

records.notes: No offset or exchange rate stated in abstract.

records.title: Proton exchange in aqueous urea solutions measured by water-exchange (WEX) NMR spectroscopy and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) imaging in vitro.
records.quote: The results showed that proton exchange in aqueous urea solutions is acid and base catalyzed with the rate constants: ka=(9.95±1.1)×106 l/(mol·s) and kb=(6.21±0.21)×106 l/(mol·s), respectively.

States that near neutral pH the urea exchange rate is minimal and could not be estimated by quantitative CEST; urea is in slow exchange, observable at 3 T. No ppm stated.

records.title: Noninvasive imaging of renal urea handling by CEST-MRI.

records.title: Delayed urea differential enhancement CEST (dudeCEST)-MRI with T1 correction for monitoring renal urea handling.

records.notes: Another sentence of the abstract writes the offset as 1.0 ppm. No exchange rate stated.

records.metabolite_or_pool: UREA NH2 (+1 ppm) and rNOE pools (-1.6, -3.5 ppm) in kidney

records.notes: Cross-listed for rNOE. No exchange rate stated.

records.title: (15)N Heteronuclear Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer MRI.

records.title: The z-spectrum from human blood at 7T.

records.title: MRI of GlycoNOE in the human liver using GraspNOE-Dixon.

records.title: In vivo reproducibility of 3D relayed NOE in the healthy human brain at 7 T.
records.quote: The mean rNOE contributions from GM and WM values were 8.9% and 9.6%, which were ∼10% of the corresponding total NOEMTR signal.
records.metabolite_or_pool: rNOE (isolated relayed-NOE contribution) in brain

known_but_not_in_abstract: 22431193 (Haris et al. 2012, NMR Biomed) — UNVERIFIED: I believe the full text gives absolute amine exchange rates at ~37 °C, pH ~7 for creatine (~950 s^-1), phosphocreatine (~140 s^-1) and ATP (~140 s^-1) plus pKa values; the abstract only states the 7-8x ratio.

30687942 (Chung et al. 2019, MRM) — UNVERIFIED: I believe the full text reports a PCr k_ex of roughly 100-150 s^-1 at pH 7.0 in phantom and places the PCr CEST peak at ~2.6 ppm; abstract gives only the <400 s^-1 upper bound and no offset.

26153196 (Lee et al. 2016, in vitro endogenous CEST agents at 3 T and 7 T) — UNVERIFIED: I believe the full text tabulates chemical shifts and exchange-rate regimes for many endogenous metabolites (including chondroitin sulfate/GAG and amine-bearing nucleotides); the abstract gives no numbers.

18268341 (Ling et al. 2008, PNAS gagCEST) — UNVERIFIED: I believe the full text assigns GAG hydroxyl protons to ~0.9-1.9 ppm (peak ~1.0 ppm) and the N-acetyl amide to ~3.2 ppm from water; the abstract gives no numbers.

31793114 (thiol-water exchange of GSH/Cys/NAC) — UNVERIFIED: I believe the full text reports the thiol resonance at roughly -2.7 ppm (upfield) and NAC thiol k_ex on the order of 10^3 s^-1 at pH 7.2/37 °C with GSH/Cys faster; only the -2.7 ppm figure is independently abstract-verified (PMID 36140239 above). Exchange rate: I do not know the exact value.

31004385 (urea WEX/CEST) — UNVERIFIED: I believe the full text reports a first-order urea k_sw minimum of a few tens of s^-1 near pH 7 at 37 °C and a urea NH2 offset of ~1.0 ppm; abstract gives only second-order catalytic constants and no offset.
40411372 (human liver 7 T five-pool fit) — UNVERIFIED: the fitted pools are presumably amide at ~3.5 ppm, guanidino at ~2.0 ppm and rNOE at ~-3.5 ppm, but the abstract does not state the offsets.
39367632 (glycoNOE in human liver) — UNVERIFIED: I believe the glycogen NOE is reported near -1 ppm (upfield) in the full text; abstract does not state it.
29111410 (human blood z-spectrum at 7 T) — the abstract says Bloch-McConnell fitting gave exchange-rate estimates for the APT and NOE pools; I do not know the values.

Carnosine/histidine IMIDAZOLE ring protons for endogenous CEST — I do not know a paper whose abstract states their exchange rate or shift from water under physiological conditions; abstract-level evidence (24719307, 39103163, 21974716) indicates diffusion-limited/very fast exchange (>10^4-10^5 s^-1), i.e., not usable as a slow/intermediate CEST pool at 3 T. records.title: MRI detection of glycogen in vivo by using chemical exchange saturation transfer imaging (glycoCEST).
records.quote: Here, we show that glycogen can be detected indirectly through the water signal by using selective radio frequency (RF) saturation of the hydroxyl protons in the 0.5- to 1.5-ppm frequency range downfield from water. The resulting saturated spins are rapidly transferred to water protons via chemical exchange, leading to partial saturation of the water signal, a process now known as chemical exchange saturation transfer. This effect is demonstrated in glycogen phantoms at magnetic field strengths of 4.7 and 9.4 T, showing improved detection at higher field in adherence with MR exchange theory. Difference images obtained during RF irradiation at 1.0 ppm upfield and downfield of the water signal showed that glycogen metabolism could be followed in isolated, perfused mouse livers at 4.7 T before and after administration of glucagon.

Honest summary for the reference table: NO abstract states a liver-tissue hydroxyl exchange rate. Abstract-stated hydroxyl k_ex values are: myo-inositol 600 s^-1 (brain paper, conditions of the k measurement unstated); 3OMG 360-670 s^-1 at pH 6.14/4 C (solution); pooled sugar hydroxyls ~1000 s^-1 at 25 C (solution, T2-derived); Ser/Thr/Tyr+Lys 700-10,000 s^-1 at pH 7/36 C (solution, catalysts raise several-fold); GAG ksw=9.2e6*10^-pH+196.9 in porcine disc in vivo at 3 T; glycogen 31,847 Hz at 37 C (solution, T2/Swift-Connick, likely not comparable). Glucose hydroxyl rates at pH 7.2/37 C exist in the literature (PMID 31313865, 37593950) but are not in any abstract. A liver simulation must therefore borrow: shifts from human-liver glycoCEST (0.5-1.5 ppm, ~1.0 ppm at 3 T) and glucose solution NMR (0.66/1.28/2.08/2.88 ppm); rates from brain (myo-inositol) or solution measurements, with the caveats that liver-tissue glycogen CEST is 'significantly less' than solution (PMID 25946616) and phosphate/pH catalysis alters hydroxyl rates (PMID 32936483, 8771020).
